title: Researching a Topic with AI

thumbnail.headline: Open Every Source
thumbnail.image: Navy background, an AI answer card with three reference links, one ticked in teal, one marked partly, one crossed out, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Open Every Source
slide.body: Answer card with three references: green tick, amber half-tick, red cross. Small tag: AI for Everyday Work · Lesson 8.

production_notes: [VERSION] Whether free tiers of Claude and ChatGPT can search the web and show links must be checked before recording. The voiceover only says 'some tools can search the web and show links'.
[REGION] Laws on flexible and hybrid work differ by country. The voiceover does not say what any law says; it only shows Mei finding that the AI's legal claim differs from the official source.
Mei and her Kuala Lumpur technology company are hypothetical. The report and statistic the AI cites in the example are fictional and must not resemble a real report title on screen.
Mei's prompt and the general research prompt appear in full on code-layout slides (scenes 9 and 6).

Hook.voiceover: You ask an AI assistant about a work topic. It gives you a clear answer with three references and a link. You click the link. It does not work. You search for the report. It does not exist.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, we summarised documents that we already had. Today, we research a topic that is new to us. AI assistants are very useful at the start of research. They can explain a topic in plain language, list the questions you should answer, suggest search terms and types of sources, and compare options at a general level.

slide.title: AI at the start of research
slide.body: Explain a topic in plain language · List questions to answer · Suggest search terms and types of sources · Compare options at a general level

Explain.voiceover: But AI is not reliable as the final source of facts. It can invent facts. It can also invent citations: report titles, authors, statistics, laws and web links that look real but do not exist. Some tools can search the web and show links, which helps. But the answer can still misreport what the source says.

slide.title: Not the final source
slide.body: Can invent facts · Can invent citations: titles, authors, statistics, laws, links · Web links help, but the answer can still misreport the source

Explain.voiceover: So research with AI in two stages. Stage one, explore with AI. Understand the topic and collect questions and search terms. Stage two, verify in original sources. For every key claim, find the original yourself. Open every link. Check that the source exists, that it is trustworthy and recent, and that it really says what the AI claimed.

slide.title: Research in two stages
slide.body: Stage 1: Explore with AI (topic, questions, search terms) → Stage 2: Verify in original sources (exists? trustworthy? recent? says the same?)

Explain.voiceover: And one simple rule. If you cannot find an original source for a claim, do not use the claim.
Here is a useful first-stage prompt. It asks for the main ideas in plain English, then a list of questions to research, and suggestions for search terms and official sources to check.

slide.title: A first-stage research prompt
slide.body: I am new to [topic]. Explain the main ideas in plain English. Then list 8 questions I should research, and suggest search terms and the types of official sources I should check.

Explain.voiceover: Think of a helpful person at a conference who tells you what they remember from many talks. They help you understand the subject and know where to look. But you would not quote them until you had read the original talk yourself.
Explain.stock_query: people chatting at professional conference break

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see this in practice. Mei is an HR officer at a technology company in Kuala Lumpur, in Malaysia. Her director asks her to research options for a hybrid-work policy.
Demonstrate.stock_query: HR officer researching at laptop Asia

Demonstrate.voiceover: She starts with a general prompt, with no company details. She asks for the common types of hybrid-work policy, the advantages and disadvantages of each, and the questions an HR team should answer before choosing one.

slide.title: Mei's prompt
slide.body: Explain the common types of hybrid-work policy for office staff, with advantages and disadvantages of each. List questions an HR team should answer before choosing one.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The answer gives her four policy types, and useful questions about fairness, equipment and team meetings. It also makes a claim about what a national law requires, and it cites a named report with a statistic about productivity. Some of this is useful, and some of it needs checking.

slide.title: What the AI gave her
slide.body: Four policy types · Questions on fairness, equipment, team meetings · A claim about a national law · A named report with a productivity statistic

Demonstrate.voiceover: Mei checks every claim before she shares her notes. The four policy types appear in guidance from professional HR bodies, so they are correct. For the legal claim, she checks the official government website. The rules are different from what the AI said, so she marks it partly correct and uses the official wording.

slide.title: Mei checks each claim
slide.body: Four policy types → found in professional HR guidance → Correct (green). Legal claim → official government website → Partly correct: use the official wording (amber).

Demonstrate.voiceover: Then the report and its statistic. She searches for the title and the authors. She cannot find the report anywhere, so she deletes the claim completely. An invented report in her notes could have misled her director. Her final notes contain only claims she has checked, and each one lists its original source.

slide.title: The missing report
slide.body: Named report and statistic → searched title and authors → Not found → Deleted (red). Final notes: only checked claims, each with its source.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The most serious mistake is copying AI references into a report without opening them. And a real link is not enough, because the page may say something different. Open every source, read the relevant part, and use only what you have confirmed.

slide.title: Before you quote it
slide.body: "Open every source. Read the relevant part. Use only what you have confirmed."

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, use AI to explore a new topic: explain it, list questions, and suggest search terms and types of sources. Second, AI can invent facts and citations, so open and check every reference and link. Third, use only claims you have confirmed in an original, trustworthy source, and record that source in your notes.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Explore with AI: ideas, questions, search terms. 2. Open and check every reference and link. 3. Use only confirmed claims; record the source.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, research a work question with public information and no company details. Choose three key claims from the answer and check each one against an original source. Mark each as correct, partly correct, or wrong. Next week, we redesign your work week, starting with Organising Your Work: Plans, Lists and Templates. See you there.
